paragraphs: Federated learning lets multiple parties collaborate without exchanging their raw data, but differences between their datasets can undermine the resulting models. This paper focuses on differences in features: the information presented to a model can have different distributions across participants. The authors argue that this issue has received less attention than differences in the distribution of labels.

Their approach, ADCOL, replaces the usual emphasis on averaging models with an adversarial training process. A server trains a discriminator to identify which party produced a representation. Meanwhile, the participating parties learn representations whose distributions are shared across parties. These opposing objectives make the distinction between participants something the representation learning process explicitly tries to reduce.

The reported experiments show better performance than state-of-the-art federated learning algorithms on non-identically distributed features. The contribution is therefore both a different collaboration mechanism and empirical evidence for its usefulness in this setting. It directs learning toward common representations when variation between participants lies in their input features.
icml-2023-adversarial-collaborative-lear.tldr: ADCOL improves collaborative learning on differing feature distributions by training participants to produce common representations through an adversarial objective.

paragraphs: Communication between clients and a central server can bottleneck federated learning. Compressing gradients reduces that traffic, but biased compression can distort optimization and lead to poor convergence. This paper studies whether error feedback, which compensates for compression errors, can address that problem in federated learning with non-convex objectives.

The authors analyze Fed-EF, a compressed federated learning scheme with two variants distinguished by the server's optimizer. They show that it can match the convergence rate of the corresponding full-precision method while achieving linear speedup with the number of clients. Experiments likewise report matching performance with substantially less communication, supporting the value of retaining and compensating for compression error.

The analysis also examines partial participation, where only some clients contribute at a time. Here, accumulated error compensation can become stale, introducing an additional slowdown factor into convergence. Experiments support this effect. The findings identify both a strong case for error feedback and a specific limitation that arises when participation is intermittent.
icml-2023-analysis-of-error-feedback-in-.tldr: Fed-EF can preserve full-precision convergence with compressed communication, but partial client participation introduces a slowdown from stale error compensation.

paragraphs: Assessing a model after its data distribution changes is difficult when the new data have no labels. One possible clue is disagreement: how often models trained with different randomness produce different predictions on the same inputs. Earlier experiments connect this measurable quantity to prediction error, suggesting a way to assess performance without target-domain labels.

The paper investigates a more specific pattern. Across models, target-domain classification error often follows a linear relationship with source-domain error. In the observed disagreement-on-the-line phenomenon, disagreement across the two domains follows that same relationship when the error relationship holds. The authors develop a theoretical framework for studying disagreement in high-dimensional random features regression and examine conditions under which this pattern arises.

Experiments on CIFAR-10-C, Tiny ImageNet-C, and Camelyon17 agree with the theory. This supports the relevance of the theoretical findings beyond the particular regression setting used for analysis. The result helps explain an empirical performance-estimation signal while treating the linear relationship as a phenomenon whose occurrence depends on conditions.
icml-2023-demystifying-disagreement-on-t.tldr: The paper develops a conditional theoretical explanation for why model disagreement can track prediction error across distribution shifts.

paragraphs: This paper addresses sequential decision making in contextual Markov decision processes where contexts can be adversarial. The goal is to control regret, the accumulated performance shortfall used to evaluate learning over episodes. Its algorithm, OMG-CMDP!, connects this decision-making problem to online prediction of rewards and environment dynamics.

The method assumes a realizable function class and access to two online regression oracles. A least-squares oracle approximates context-dependent rewards, while a log-loss oracle approximates context-dependent dynamics. The algorithm is computationally efficient if these regression oracles are efficient, making the efficiency claim explicitly dependent on the prediction tools available. The authors also describe the method as robust to approximation errors.

The regret guarantee depends on episode count, horizon, state and action counts, and the combined regret of the two regression oracles. This makes the quality of online function approximation part of the decision-making guarantee. The authors claim, to their knowledge, the first efficient rate-optimal result for adversarial contextual MDPs under this standard online function approximation assumption.
icml-2023-efficient-rate-optimal-regret-.tldr: OMG-CMDP! achieves rate-optimal regret in adversarial contextual MDPs under realizability and access to suitable online regression oracles.

paragraphs: Neural networks can achieve different accuracies across subgroups, and fairness objectives often address this by constraining final outputs. This paper examines the internal decision process as well. Its central question is whether a network relies on aligned decision rationales across subgroups, even when its final predictions have been regularized for fairness.

The authors introduce a parameter parity score that measures neuron influence across subgroups. Their empirical studies suggest that misaligned decision rationales could contribute to unfairness, and that existing output-focused regularizers fail to align intermediate neurons. They formulate a new objective requiring consistency across both internal processing and final prediction, then relax that objective into a practical optimization method called gradient-guided parity alignment.

The method encourages neurons to behave consistently across subgroups, with gradients determining how that consistency is weighted. Experiments across several datasets report substantial fairness improvements while maintaining high accuracy and outperforming competing approaches. The work provides evidence that examining how a network reaches decisions can offer an additional route to improving fairness.
icml-2023-fairer-fairness-as-decision-ra.tldr: FAIRER improves fairness by encouraging subgroup consistency in influential neurons throughout a network, alongside its final predictions.

paragraphs: Large autoregressive models ordinarily generate tokens sequentially, requiring another model run for each token. This creates a speed bottleneck even when substantial parallel computing capacity is available. The paper introduces speculative decoding to generate several tokens concurrently while preserving the large model's output distribution.

The approach relies on the observation that some portions of a difficult language-modeling task are easier to approximate than others. More efficient models produce candidate continuations, and the large model processes those candidates in parallel. A sampling procedure makes this speculative computation compatible with exact sampling from the large model, so the approximation can accelerate generation without changing the target distribution.

The method works with existing models and does not require retraining or changes to their architecture. On T5-XXL, the authors report a two- to threefold acceleration over the standard T5X implementation, with identical outputs. This demonstration shows that changing the decoding procedure can yield a substantial speed improvement while retaining the original model's generation behavior.
icml-2023-fast-inference-from-transforme.tldr: Speculative decoding uses efficient approximation models and parallel verification to accelerate generation while preserving the large model's output distribution.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning uses negative examples when learning representations, and practical success often involves using many of them. Existing generalization bounds create a tension with that practice: they grow linearly with the number of negatives, making the theoretical guarantee worse as that number increases. This paper develops bounds that largely remove that dependence.

The new guarantees depend on the number of negative examples only through logarithmic terms. The analysis combines empirical covering numbers and Rademacher complexities, mathematical tools for controlling the richness of a learning system, with the Lipschitz continuity of its loss. These ingredients allow a sharper account of how the training objective relates to generalization.

For self-bounding Lipschitz losses, the authors derive stronger, optimistic bounds that yield fast rates under a low-noise condition. They also specialize the analysis to linear representations and deep neural network representations. The contribution is a more informative theoretical explanation of contrastive learning, including conditional improvements that distinguish favorable learning settings from the general case.
icml-2023-generalization-analysis-for-co.tldr: New contrastive-learning generalization bounds remove linear dependence on the number of negatives and give faster rates under additional favorable conditions.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations describe changes associated with a different model decision, but most methods explain individual cases. Understanding broader model behavior often requires collecting many such local explanations. This paper argues that this route does not adequately resolve reliability and computational cost, particularly when practitioners need efficient, interactive tools.

GLOBE-CE is a framework for global counterfactual explanations built around feature translations. It addresses scalability and reliability concerns that become especially relevant for higher-dimensional datasets and continuous features. The authors also develop a mathematical analysis of translations involving categorical features and incorporate that analysis into the method, extending the treatment beyond purely continuous changes.

Evaluations on public datasets and user studies report significant improvements over the current state of the art across multiple measures, including speed and reliability. The significance is that global explanation becomes a direct methodological target. Rather than relying solely on the accumulation of individual explanations, the framework provides a structured approach to examining counterfactual behavior more broadly.
icml-2023-globe-ce-a-translation-based-a.tldr: GLOBE-CE uses feature translations to produce global counterfactual explanations with empirically improved speed and reliability.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent often finds neural networks that generalize well, but explaining why remains difficult. This paper identifies an implicit regularization effect on the logit-weight Jacobian norm. That quantity describes the sensitivity of a network's prediction scores to changes in its weights, connecting the training procedure to how strongly those scores respond to parameter changes.

The effect is weighted by the impurity of the network's probability output. Consequently, its influence is tied to the state of the predictions and becomes active during a particular phase of training. This qualification matters: the proposed explanation describes a training-dependent effect, rather than a penalty that acts with the same strength throughout optimization.

Using this finding, the authors design an optimization method that explicitly regularizes the Jacobian norm. They report performance similar to other state-of-the-art sharpness-aware optimization methods. The paper therefore connects an analysis of SGD's implicit behavior to a concrete training objective, showing how a proposed explanation of generalization can motivate an explicit optimizer.
icml-2023-implicit-jacobian-regularizati.tldr: The paper identifies a prediction-dependent Jacobian regularization effect in SGD and uses it to design an explicit optimization method.

paragraphs: In Gaussian process models with non-conjugate likelihoods, approximating the posterior and learning hyperparameters become intertwined. The objective used for approximate inference can therefore also influence which model settings are selected. This paper examines whether one objective is equally suitable for both tasks and develops a training procedure that treats them differently.

The authors find that variational inference's lower bound on marginal likelihood is suitable for constructing the approximate posterior. For hyperparameter optimization, however, they show that a more direct approximation to marginal likelihood, as used in expectation propagation, provides a better learning objective. Their hybrid procedure uses conjugate-computation variational inference for inference and an expectation-propagation-like objective for hyperparameter learning.

They compare the hybrid approach with variational inference, expectation propagation, and the Laplace approximation across a wide range of datasets. The results empirically support its effectiveness. The main contribution is a deliberate division of responsibilities: posterior approximation and hyperparameter selection can use different objectives within the same training procedure.
icml-2023-improving-hyperparameter-learn.tldr: A hybrid Gaussian process training procedure combines variational posterior inference with an expectation-propagation-like objective for better hyperparameter learning.

paragraphs: Vision models commonly adapt a general-purpose model trained on a large, fixed image collection. This paper explores a different approach: actively find training images on the web that are useful for a particular target dataset. The motivation is that a static pretraining collection contains only a limited snapshot of the visual information available online.

Internet Explorer repeatedly searches for images using text queries, downloads them, and trains through self-supervision. It then assesses which images were useful and uses that information to prioritize future searches. Data collection and representation learning form a feedback loop, allowing the training material to become progressively more relevant to the target.

Across several datasets, the method matches or exceeds the reported CLIP oracle performance after actively querying the Internet for 30–40 hours on a desktop with one GPU. These findings support targeted web exploration as a practical way to train a small-scale model for a desired dataset. The demonstrated strength lies in directing data acquisition toward the task.
icml-2023-internet-explorer-targeted-rep.tldr: Internet Explorer alternates web search and self-supervised training to build task-focused visual representations on a single-GPU desktop.

paragraphs: Learning an inverse normally benefits from examples pairing inputs with outputs. Iterative inversion instead assumes access to the forward function and samples of the outputs one wants to produce. Its main challenge is that outputs from an initial random guess can differ substantially from the desired output distribution. The authors prove that their procedure can guide learning correctly under strict conditions on the function.

For control, desired behavior is supplied through video embeddings of trajectories without action labels. The method repeatedly learns to imitate trajectories produced by its current policy with added random exploration noise. This approach uses supervised learning without requiring rewards, connecting the inverse-learning formulation to learning behavior from observations.

The authors combine a VQ-VAE trajectory embedding with a transformer policy and demonstrate non-trivial continuous control on several tasks. They also report improved imitation of diverse behaviors compared with reward-based methods. The theoretical guarantee remains conditional, while the control experiments show how the iterative procedure can work with expressive trajectory and policy representations.
icml-2023-learning-control-by-iterative-.tldr: Iterative inversion learns control from action-free behavioral demonstrations using supervised updates and exploration, with inverse-learning guarantees under strict conditions.

paragraphs: Numerical solvers for partial differential equations often depend on solving associated linear systems efficiently. In preconditioned conjugate gradient methods, the quality of the preconditioner strongly affects performance. Designing one by traditional numerical techniques can require substantial problem-specific expertise and careful matrix operations, motivating a learned approach.

The paper learns an approximate factorization of the system matrix for use as a preconditioner. It represents preconditioners with graph neural networks, drawing on the observation that both preconditioners and neural PDE solvers can supply approximate solutions at relatively low computational cost. The authors also introduce a loss that reformulates traditional preconditioner measures to incorporate information from the distribution of PDE data.

Experiments on various two- and three-dimensional linear second-order PDEs demonstrate effectiveness and generalizability. The approach places learning inside an established numerical solver through a component that determines its efficiency. Its training objective also makes the PDE data distribution relevant to preconditioner design, providing a route to learning useful numerical structure from examples.
icml-2023-learning-preconditioners-for-c.tldr: The method learns graph-based matrix factorizations that serve as effective preconditioners for conjugate-gradient PDE solvers.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks are often evaluated against the expressive power of the first Weisfeiler–Lehman procedure, or 1-WL. Methods that go beyond this reference can sacrifice efficiency or apply only to particular graph types. This paper approaches the problem through graph search, examining what structural information classical search procedures can contribute to learned graph representations.

The authors propose a vertex-colouring scheme and show that search algorithms can efficiently compute representations exceeding 1-WL. The scheme inherits structural properties of graph search that can help with problems such as graph biconnectivity. They also establish that, under certain conditions, increasing the radius of the searched neighborhood produces a hierarchy of increasing expressive power.

The paper develops graph neural networks using breadth-first and depth-first search to investigate the scheme further. These variants expose graph properties that can be captured beyond 1-WL. The contribution connects familiar search procedures to stronger graph representations while explicitly qualifying the conditions under which a larger search neighborhood increases expressivity.
icml-2023-local-vertex-colouring-graph-n.tldr: Search-based vertex colouring gives graph neural networks expressive power beyond 1-WL, with a conditional hierarchy as search neighborhoods expand.

paragraphs: Offline decision learning often has to work with imperfect recorded experience. Some trajectories have rewards while others do not; rewarded trajectories may lack actions or demonstrate poor behavior; and the dataset may cover only part of the environment. The paper brings these situations together under offline policy learning from observations, encompassing several reinforcement and imitation learning setups.

MAHALO learns a policy by optimizing a lower bound on performance that accounts for uncertainty from incomplete data coverage. It constructs this bound through adversarial training of critic and reward functions that remain consistent with the dataset. This pessimistic approach pushes the policy to remain robust to deficiencies in the available evidence.

The authors report that MAHALO consistently matches or outperforms specialized methods across a variety of tasks, with theoretical and experimental support. Its significance is a common framework for learning from datasets with different combinations of missing information and imperfect demonstrations. The uncertainty caused by inadequate coverage becomes part of the optimization objective.
icml-2023-mahalo-unifying-offline-reinfo.tldr: MAHALO unifies offline reinforcement and imitation learning by optimizing conservative performance estimates under incomplete and imperfect trajectory data.

paragraphs: Universal approximation asks whether a neural network family can approximate every function in a specified class arbitrarily well. This paper studies how narrow leaky-ReLU networks can be when depth is unrestricted. Its target is uniform approximation of continuous functions on a compact domain, where the approximation must be accurate throughout the domain.

The authors derive the exact minimum width: max(d_x + 1, d_y), with one additional unit when d_y equals d_x + 1. Here d_x and d_y are the input and output dimensions. The formula shows that the output dimension affects the threshold, including a special case that requires more width than the maximum expression alone would indicate.

To prove the result, the paper introduces a lift-flow-discretization approach and connects uniform approximation to topology. The result distinguishes this setting from earlier approximation guarantees for Lp functions at the critical width max(d_x, d_y). It establishes a precise architectural threshold for representational capability under the stated approximation criterion and unrestricted depth.
icml-2023-minimum-width-of-leaky-relu-ne.tldr: The paper establishes the exact minimum width for uniform universal approximation by arbitrarily deep leaky-ReLU networks on compact domains.

paragraphs: Exploration can improve a reinforcement learning policy while temporarily reducing performance. This paper studies how to maintain a performance threshold in every episode of a finite-state, finite-action episodic Markov decision process. The initial setting assumes access to a known safe baseline policy that the learner can use while exploring.

StepMix adaptively blends that baseline with an optimistic policy, smoothly adjusting their contribution. The authors prove that the resulting strategy satisfies the episode-wise conservative constraint with high probability and achieves a near-optimal regret order comparable to the unconstrained setting. A second method, EpsMix, uses randomization and receives the same performance guarantee.

The paper also considers learning the baseline from offline data. Similar conservative guarantees and regret results hold when that dataset is sufficiently large. Experiments support the theory and the effectiveness of both exploration strategies. The findings show that stringent per-episode constraints can coexist with strong learning rates in the analyzed setting, with explicit qualifications on probability and available baseline information.
icml-2023-near-optimal-conservative-expl.tldr: StepMix and EpsMix achieve near-optimal regret while maintaining episode-wise performance constraints with high probability under the stated baseline assumptions.

paragraphs: Automatic differentiation is known to be almost always correct over real-valued parameter spaces in a precise mathematical sense. Actual neural network programs use machine-representable parameters, however, so this paper studies correctness on that parameter set. It separates points where a derivative exists but automatic differentiation returns the wrong result from points where the network has no ordinary derivative.

For networks with bias parameters, the authors prove that the first set is empty: at differentiable parameter points, automatic differentiation computes the derivative correctly. They also derive a tight bound on the size of the non-differentiable set, growing linearly with the number of non-differentiabilities in the activation functions, and give an exact criterion for membership in that set.

At non-differentiable points, automatic differentiation still returns a Clarke subderivative, a generalized derivative suitable for describing non-smooth functions. The paper also extends its analysis to networks that may lack biases. Together, these results give a more precise account of correctness when parameters come from machine-representable numbers.
icml-2023-on-the-correctness-of-automati.tldr: For networks with biases and machine-representable parameters, automatic differentiation returns correct derivatives where they exist and Clarke subderivatives at non-smooth points.

paragraphs: GPU simulation can collect reinforcement learning experience extremely quickly, but a learning algorithm must keep pace to benefit. On-policy methods such as PPO have been popular because they scale readily. Off-policy methods use samples more efficiently, yet their scaling difficulties can leave them slower in elapsed training time.

Parallel Q-Learning addresses this mismatch by parallelizing data collection, policy learning, and value learning. The scheme is designed specifically for massively parallel GPU simulation on a single workstation. Its organization targets the full learning process, so faster simulation can be accompanied by parallel work on the policy and its value estimates.

The reported experiments show better wall-clock training time than PPO while retaining superior sample efficiency. They demonstrate Q-learning with tens of thousands of parallel environments and investigate how environment count, exploration, batch size, and GPU choice affect learning speed. The findings show that sample-efficient off-policy learning can also be fast in elapsed time when its execution is organized for this simulation setting.
icml-2023-parallel-q-learning-scaling-of.tldr: Parallel Q-Learning coordinates simulation, policy learning, and value learning to outperform PPO in elapsed training time while retaining better sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Detecting anomalies in multivariate time series requires learning normal patterns across several changing variables. Existing methods can depend on learning a fixed set of mappings for each series, which the authors associate with expensive computation and limited adaptation. PUAD instead models multiple time series through distributions over a shared collection of prototypes.

These prototypes represent diverse normal temporal patterns. To learn and regulate them, the method combines reconstruction-based anomaly detection with prototype-oriented optimal transport inside a probabilistic dynamical generative framework powered by a Transformer. This brings the representation of normal behavior and the organization of prototypes into one learning approach.

The prototypes are meta-learned to be transferable, allowing the model to adapt to new multivariate time series. Experiments on five public datasets support the method's effectiveness. The central contribution is reusable normal-pattern structure: representing different series through transferable prototypes provides a way to address adaptation without relying entirely on separate fixed mappings for every series.
icml-2023-prototype-oriented-unsupervise.tldr: PUAD learns transferable prototypes of normal temporal behavior to support unsupervised anomaly detection and adaptation across multivariate time series.

paragraphs: Answering a question about a scientific article can require more than locating a fact. QASA targets questions that demand deeper understanding and reasoning. A think-aloud study identified surface, testing, and deep questions, informing a benchmark of 1,798 new question-answer pairs about artificial intelligence and machine learning articles.

The proposed answering approach draws on a distinction between gathering relevant knowledge and reasoning from evidence. It organizes a large language model's work into associative selection, generation of an evidence-based rationale, and systematic composition of the answer. This makes the reasoning process an explicit part of the approach rather than leaving the entire task as an undifferentiated response.

Experiments report a large improvement over InstructGPT, and the authors identify rationale generation as critical to that gain. The result supports the usefulness of explicitly connecting selected information to an evidential explanation before composing an answer. The paper contributes both a benchmark for advanced scientific question answering and an approach designed around its reasoning demands.
icml-2023-qasa-advanced-question-answeri.tldr: QASA introduces a scientific question-answering benchmark and a staged reasoning approach whose evidence-based rationales are critical to its reported gains.

paragraphs: Posterior inference estimates a distribution over model parameters after observing data. Generative models offer a way to represent such distributions, but assessing whether their inferred posteriors are accurate is difficult. This paper introduces Tests of Accuracy with Random Points, or TARP, to examine generative posterior estimators through coverage testing.

TARP estimates coverage probabilities using a sampling-based approach. This distinguishes it from earlier coverage methods that require evaluating the posterior itself. The authors prove a necessary-and-sufficient characterization of posterior accuracy for their approach, giving the test a theoretical connection to whether the estimated distribution is correct.

Demonstrations on synthetic examples show that TARP can assess posterior inference in high-dimensional spaces. The authors also report cases where it detects inaccurate inference that existing methods miss. These findings make the method relevant to both likelihood-based and simulation-based inference. Its contribution combines a theoretical accuracy criterion with evidence that sampling-based testing can reveal errors in practical posterior estimates.
icml-2023-sampling-based-accuracy-testin.tldr: TARP uses sampling-based coverage tests to assess generative posterior accuracy, with a necessary-and-sufficient theoretical criterion and demonstrations in high dimensions.

paragraphs: Anytime neural networks adjust their computational complexity during execution to fit available hardware resources. Their design therefore has to support useful predictions at different computational budgets. The paper argues that manually designed networks are constrained by designers' experience and can leave better solutions unexplored.

The authors model the training process as a discrete-time Markov chain. They use that analysis to identify network paths that contribute most to training, then build TIPS, a framework for automatically designing anytime networks under different hardware constraints. The key idea is to use the structure of training paths as evidence for design decisions.

Experiments show improvements in convergence rate and test accuracy. Compared with existing anytime-network approaches, the paper reports accuracy gains of 2%–6.6% across multiple datasets and state-of-the-art tradeoffs between accuracy and floating-point operation counts. These results support the use of training-path analysis to guide automatic architecture design, with benefits measured both in prediction quality and computational tradeoffs.
icml-2023-tips-topologically-important-p.tldr: TIPS uses a Markov-chain analysis of training paths to automatically design anytime networks with improved accuracy and computational tradeoffs.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a transformer infer from examples supplied in its prompt. This paper formalizes that behavior as learning an algorithm: at inference time, the transformer implicitly constructs a hypothesis function from the examples. This perspective makes it possible to study the statistical behavior of the procedure implemented by the model.

Using a multitask-learning framework, the authors derive generalization bounds for prompts containing either independent input-label pairs or trajectories from a dynamical system. Their analysis connects excess risk to algorithmic stability, which concerns how the learned procedure responds to changes in its examples. They identify conditions under which transformer and attention architectures satisfy the required stability property and provide empirical verification.

For previously unseen tasks, the paper identifies a relationship between transfer risk, task complexity, and the number of training tasks. Numerical evaluations show that transformers can implement near-optimal algorithms on classical regression problems with independent and dynamic data. These results support both the algorithm-learning interpretation and the theory's predictions about stability and transfer.
icml-2023-transformers-as-algorithms-gen.tldr: The paper treats in-context learning as algorithm learning and connects transformer generalization to stability, task complexity, and multitask training.

paragraphs: An agent operating across changing environments benefits from behaviors that preserve useful shared structure. Unsupervised skill discovery seeks such behaviors without a reward function, but earlier approaches often focused on stationary environments or kept the trained skill fixed within each episode. This paper develops a method intended to represent structure shared across environmental changes.

The algorithm learns skills incrementally. Each new skill is encouraged to extend the states reachable through compositions of skills already learned. This gives skill discovery a cumulative objective: new behavior should expand what the existing collection can accomplish. A separate evaluation process aims to prevent redundant skills from accumulating in that collection.

Experiments in changing maze-navigation and locomotion environments show that the resulting skills represent shared structure. The authors also demonstrate greater usefulness than baseline skills on downstream tasks. The contribution is a way to build and assess reusable behavior over time, with state-coverage expansion and redundancy control providing complementary guidance for what should be added.
icml-2023-unsupervised-skill-discovery-f.tldr: The method incrementally discovers reusable skills by expanding the coverage of existing skill compositions and screening for redundancy.
